sentences.text: Mymoorapelta is one of the smaller nodosaurids, with the largest known individual reaching about 3 meters in length.
This dinosaur possessed a narrow snout and an almost triangular skull featuring two large backward-pointing horns from the brow and two additional horns pointing backward and downward from the jugal.
The premaxillae likely formed a narrow, toothed, and trapezoidal muzzle similar to that of Gargoyleosaurus.
Five different armor types were observed, including elongated spines and a massive sacral shield constructed from tiny bony plates.
Fossils of Mymoorapelta were first discovered in the Mygatt-Moore Quarry in 1990.
Over 160 fossil elements have been found scattered over 25 meters of the 150 square meter Mygatt-Moore Quarry.
The holotype specimen, which serves as the basis for the species description, includes a left ilium with preserved bitemarks.
James Kirkland and Kenneth Carpenter initially described Mymoorapelta in 1994, naming the type species Mymoorapelta maysi.
Mymoorapelta was a low browser that fed on cycads and conifers.
This low-browsing herbivore likely consumed ferns, cycads, and conifers.
Nodosaurid teeth, including those of Mymoorapelta, were blade-like, larger, and more complex than ankylosaurid teeth, featuring rough enamel and a crenelated cingulum.
Unlike club-tailed ankylosaurids, Mymoorapelta had a tail with spikes likely used for defense.
The clade Nodosauridae was named in 1890 by Othniel Charles Marsh, who designated Nodosaurus as the type genus.
Nodosaurids differ from ankylosaurids by having osteoderm-lined, flexible tails and sacral shields, whereas ankylosaurids evolved more recently and lack mace-like tail clubs.
Mymoorapelta lived during the Late Jurassic, approximately 155 to 150 million years ago.
Fossils of Mymoorapelta have been found in the Morrison Formation in western Colorado and central Utah.
Mymoorapelta has a limited known distribution found at two sites in Western Colorado, plus the Hanksville-Burpee and potential Albuquerque specimens.
Taphonomy of the Hanksville-Burpee specimen suggests Mymoorapelta died inland, contrary to previous inferences of a coastal distribution for nodosaurids.
It is debated whether an osteoderm from New Mexico belongs to Mymoorapelta, as it is morphologically similar but stratigraphically closer to Gargoyleosaurus.
Researchers suggest that category 1 sacral shields might represent a growth stage of category 2 shields, similar to traits seen in modern armadillos and alligators.

It is debated whether Mymoorapelta may be an ankylosaur outside both Nodosauridae and Ankylosauridae, and there is currently some controversy regarding the position of this ankylosaurian within Ankylosauria.
